introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Pure Mathematics with Mechanics, Paper 3 (0765/3), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Time allowed: three hours.**

Full marks may be obtained for answers to ALL questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Mathematical formulae booklet published by the GCE Board are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving the answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. Start each question on a fresh page.
enonce_intro_markdown:
A particle $P$ is projected from a point $O$ on a horizontal plane at time $t = 0$ with velocity $(5\mathbf{i} + 5\sqrt3\,\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, where $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are unit vectors along $Ox$ and $Oy$ respectively.

(Take $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.)

Find,
incertitudes: Le sujet n'imprime pas de total de points par question ; l'énoncé dit seulement « All questions carry equal marks ». Les points imprimés par partie somment à 13 pour chacune des 8 questions (total 104) ; `points` de l'exercice est laissé vide.

Question 5 (c) : avec les données imprimées (g = 10, vitesse initiale 5i + 5 sqrt3 j), le temps de vol est sqrt3 = 1.73 s < 2 s : à t = 2 s la particule aurait déjà atteint le plan horizontal. Le sujet est donc physiquement incohérent si le plan est infini. Le corrigé donne la valeur des équations du vol libre (10.35 m, y = 10 sqrt3 - 20 < 0) comme réponse attendue, et signale l'autre lecture (particule arrêtée au sol à 8.66 m de O). L'intention de l'examinateur n'est pas vérifiable.
Question 5 : le sujet imprime « Take g as 10 m s^-2 » : valeur retenue g = 10. Coquille du sujet (« are are unit vectors ») : transcrite « are unit vectors ».

questions.enonce_markdown: the cartesian equation of the trajectory of $P$,
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Set-up.** Origin $O$; $Ox$ horizontal, $Oy$ vertically upwards (so the acceleration is $-g\mathbf{j}$, with $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ as printed). Neglect air resistance. Initial velocity components: $u_x = 5$, $u_y = 5\sqrt3$ (speed $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal).

**Position at time $t$** (constant acceleration):

$$x = 5t,\qquad y = 5\sqrt3\,t - \tfrac12(10)t^2 = 5\sqrt3\,t - 5t^2$$

Eliminate $t = \dfrac{x}{5}$:

$$y = 5\sqrt3\cdot\frac{x}{5} - 5\cdot\frac{x^2}{25} = \sqrt3\,x - \frac{x^2}{5}$$

**Cartesian equation of the trajectory: $y = \sqrt3\,x - \dfrac{x^2}{5}$** (a parabola).

questions.enonce_markdown: the maximum height which $P$ attains above the horizontal plane through $O$,
questions.corrige_markdown:
At the greatest height the vertical component of velocity is zero. With the vertical motion $v_y = 5\sqrt3 - 10t$:

$$v_y = 0\;\Longrightarrow\; t = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ \mathrm{s}$$

$$H = 5\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} - 5\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2 = 7.5 - 3.75 = 3.75\ \mathrm{m}$$

**Check** with $v^2 = u^2 - 2gs$ in the vertical direction: $0 = (5\sqrt3)^2 - 2(10)H \Rightarrow H = \dfrac{75}{20} = 3.75\ \mathrm{m}$. (It is also the maximum of $y = \sqrt3x - x^2/5$, reached at $x = \tfrac{5\sqrt3}{2}$.)

**Maximum height $= 3.75\ \mathrm{m}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown: the distance of $P$ from the point $O$ when $t = 2\ \mathrm{s}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the position equations of part (a) at $t = 2$:

$$x = 5\times 2 = 10\ \mathrm{m},\qquad y = 5\sqrt3\times 2 - 5\times 2^2 = 10\sqrt3 - 20 \approx -2.68\ \mathrm{m}$$

Distance from $O$:

$$OP = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{100 + (10\sqrt3 - 20)^2} = \sqrt{100 + 700 - 400\sqrt3} = \sqrt{800 - 400\sqrt3}\approx 10.35\ \mathrm{m}$$

**Distance from $O$ at $t = 2\ \mathrm{s}$: $\approx 10.35\ \mathrm{m}$** (from the free-flight equations).

**Remark on the data.** The time of flight back to the level of $O$ is $\dfrac{2u_y}{g} = \sqrt3 \approx 1.73\ \mathrm{s}$, which is less than $2\ \mathrm{s}$; the value $y \approx -2.68\ \mathrm{m}$ means the point lies below the level of $O$. The answer above is therefore valid only if the particle continues its free flight below the level of $O$ (the plane does not stop it, for example because the plane ends before $x = 10$). If instead the particle is stopped by the plane at $t = \sqrt3\ \mathrm{s}$, it is then at rest at the range $5\sqrt3 \approx 8.66\ \mathrm{m}$ from $O$.
